buildUp: Start with the qubits: superconducting circuits patterned on a chip, which must be colder than about a tenth of a kelvin even to work as qubits and far colder to work well.

No single cooler reaches that, so cooling is staged: a pulse-tube cooler takes plates to about 50 K and 4 K, then a dilution unit takes the bottom plates to below 1 K, about 0.1 K and finally about 10 mK.

Each colder stage has much less cooling power, from watts at the top to microwatts at the bottom, so heat must be caught as high up as possible: plates hang on thin, poorly conducting posts, and nested shields catch the infrared glow of warmer surfaces.
Air would carry heat in, so the whole stack sits inside a vacuum can, and magnetic shields round the chip keep out the Earth's field.

The qubits are controlled by microwave pulses, but the cables that carry them also carry heat and noise, so each line is anchored at every plate and passed through attenuators that soak up warm noise while the strong signal survives.

Reading the answer means catching an extremely faint microwave echo, so one-way isolators stop noise travelling back down and low-noise amplifiers boost the signal before it climbs out to room-temperature electronics.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Build artificial atoms out of superconducting circuits on a chip, whose quantum states you can steer with microwave pulses, then hide them in the coldest, quietest place you can make. A dilution refrigerator cools the chip to about a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero, and every wire and shield on the way down is arranged to stop heat and noise reaching it while still letting signals in and out.

hardParts.title: Keeping qubits coherent long enough
hardParts.why: Anything that can absorb a qubit's energy or nudge its frequency destroys the computation: tiny defects in the chip's materials, stray infrared light, trapped magnetic vortices or resonances in the metal box around it. Getting qubits to last a few hundred microseconds took years of work on materials, chip design and packaging, and errors are still common enough that large useful machines will need error correction spread across many physical qubits.

hardParts.title: Wiring a chip at 10 mK to a 300 K world
hardParts.why: Every qubit needs control and readout lines, and every line is a path for heat and noise into a stage that can only remove microwatts. Today's machines with a hundred or so qubits already need hundreds of coaxial lines, each cooled and attenuated at every plate, so simply getting wires into the fridge is one of the main limits on making processors bigger.

hardParts.title: Hearing a whisper from the qubits
hardParts.why: The readout signal is a microwave tone carrying only a handful of photons, far weaker than the noise from warm electronics above. It has to be passed upward through one-way isolators and amplified by devices that add almost no noise of their own, all without letting the amplifiers' own noise leak back down to disturb the qubits.

principles.explanation: A quantum algorithm steers wave-like amplitudes so that wrong answers cancel and right ones reinforce; it does not simply try every answer at once, which is why only some problems speed up. An ordinary bit is 0 or 1. A qubit can be in a blend of both, described by two numbers called amplitudes, which act like waves that can add up or cancel out. Join n qubits together and the state needs 2 to the power n amplitudes: 50 qubits already need about a million billion numbers to describe. The algorithm is a carefully choreographed sequence of operations that does this cancelling, so that a measurement at the end is likely to give a useful result.
principles.title: Superposition and interference

principles.explanation: A tiny superconducting circuit, cooled almost to absolute zero, has quantum energy levels like an atom, and a Josephson junction spaces them unevenly so its lowest two can serve as the qubit's 0 and 1. A loop of capacitor and inductor is an electrical pendulum: charge sloshes back and forth at a set frequency, here a few billion times a second, in the microwave range. In a superconductor current flows with no resistance, so that oscillation doesn't die away quickly, and at very low temperature its energy can only take set steps, like the rungs of a ladder. A Josephson junction, an insulating barrier only a few atoms thick, makes the rungs unevenly spaced, so a pulse tuned to the bottom step moves the circuit between its lowest two levels without kicking it higher.
principles.title: A superconducting circuit as an artificial atom

principles.explanation: A qubit's energy gap is so small that room-temperature heat would flip it constantly, so the chip has to be cooled to around a hundredth of a kelvin. Heat is random jiggling, with a typical energy proportional to temperature. A qubit at about 5 GHz has an energy gap equivalent to roughly a quarter of a kelvin, more than a thousand times smaller than room temperature, about 300 K. At around 10 to 15 thousandths of a kelvin, heat has only a small fraction of the energy needed, so the qubit stays settled in its lowest state until you deliberately drive it. Even then, qubits typically keep their state for only tens to a few hundred microseconds, enough for perhaps a few thousand operations of tens of nanoseconds each.
principles.title: Why it must be so cold

principles.explanation: The fridge cools by letting helium-3 dissolve from one liquid layer into another, which absorbs heat like evaporation and keeps working almost to absolute zero. Below about 0.87 K, a mixture of helium-3 and helium-4 separates into two liquid layers, a bit like oil and water. Helium-3 atoms moving from the rich layer into the dilute one absorb heat, just as molecules escaping from a liquid as it evaporates do. What keeps it going is that the dilute layer still holds about 6.6 percent helium-3 however cold it gets, so the 'evaporation' never stops. Pumping helium-3 out of the dilute side at the still, then returning it, keeps the cycle running continuously.
principles.title: Cooling by dissolving helium

firstPrinciples.problem: Compute with quantum systems directly, to crack problems that overwhelm ordinary computers, while protecting quantum states so fragile that the slightest warmth or noise wipes them out. Some problems, like simulating how the electrons in a molecule behave, get exponentially harder for ordinary computers as they grow, because every extra particle doubles the number of possibilities to keep track of. Nature itself handles those possibilities effortlessly. But quantum states are fantastically fragile: the slightest warmth, stray radio wave or magnetic field leaks information into the surroundings and wipes the computation out, yet you still have to control and read them from a noisy, room-temperature world.

questions.answer: A good electrical conductor is usually also a good heat conductor, so copper would pour heat from room temperature straight onto the coldest stages. Instead the lines use poorer heat conductors, or superconductors that carry current but little heat, and are clamped to each plate on the way down.
questions.question: Why can't you just make the control cables out of good copper all the way down?

questions.answer: Room-temperature electronics send noise down the line along with the pulses. An attenuator cuts both by the same factor and adds only the small noise of its own cold temperature, so sending a stronger pulse and cutting it down leaves the signal intact but the noise far smaller.
questions.question: Why do the control lines deliberately throw away most of their signal with attenuators?

questions.answer: Measuring the qubits gives only one string of 0s and 1s, with probabilities set by the amplitudes. The amplitudes themselves can't be read off directly, so algorithms must use interference to concentrate probability on the answer you want.
questions.question: If 300 qubits can describe more amplitudes than there are atoms in the observable universe, why can't you just read them all out?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The striking thing is that the computer itself is a fingernail-sized chip; nearly everything you see is there to make one place in the universe cold and quiet enough. Engineers turned a curiosity of helium physics into a machine that reliably holds a chip around 10 thousandths of a degree above absolute zero for weeks, while hundreds of cables pass through it, and that is what lets electrical circuits you can see under a microscope behave like single atoms.

name: Quantum Computer
overview:
The famous golden 'chandelier' isn't the computer; it's the refrigerator. The actual processor is a chip a centimetre or two across at the very bottom, holding dozens to hundreds of qubits made from tiny superconducting circuits. They only behave as qubits when they are colder than deep space, around 10 to 15 thousandths of a degree above absolute zero, where the slightest heat or stray radio wave would scramble their delicate quantum states.

Getting there takes stages. A pulse-tube cooler at the top uses pulses of helium gas to chill the upper plates to about 50 and then 4 degrees above absolute zero. Below that, a dilution unit does the rest: a mixture of two kinds of helium, helium-3 and helium-4, is coaxed to separate, and helium-3 atoms crossing from one phase into the other soak up heat, a bit like sweat evaporating. Each plate down the chandelier is colder than the one above, and every wire is cooled and filtered at every stage so it doesn't carry heat or noise to the chip.

Programs run as precisely shaped microwave pulses sent down coaxial lines; the qubits' answers come back as faint microwave echoes, boosted by special amplifiers before they leave the fridge. Around the whole stack, nested cans shield it from heat radiation and magnetic fields, and an outer vacuum can keeps out the air.

parts.description: Stainless-steel top flange at room temperature that the whole stack hangs from; every wire and pipe enters through it.

details.didYouKnow: Many fridges hang from a frame that is isolated from the floor, because footsteps and building vibrations can shake heat into the coldest stages and disturb the qubits.
details.howItWorks: The top plate is the boundary between the lab and the cold world below. It is usually bolted to a sturdy frame, and every plate, shield and cable in the chandelier ultimately hangs from it. Its ports carry the pulse-tube cold head, the pumping lines for the helium mixture, and sealed connectors for the microwave and DC wiring, all of which must pass in without letting any air leak into the vacuum.
keyNumbers: Sits at roughly 295 K, ordinary room temperature
Typically dozens of ports and feedthroughs
Supports a cold stack that can weigh tens to hundreds of kilograms
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, often machined as a thick flange with rubber or metal seals around each port. Steel is strong, does not rust, and lets very little gas seep through, which matters when the space beneath must hold a high vacuum for months.

parts.name: Room-temperature plate

parts.description: First cold stage, chilled by the pulse-tube cooler to about 50 degrees above absolute zero.

details.didYouKnow: At this temperature nitrogen and oxygen freeze solid, so any stray air molecules in the vacuum stick to cold surfaces as frost, which actually helps keep the vacuum clean.
details.howItWorks: The 50 K plate is bolted to the first stage of the pulse-tube cooler and acts as the first heat sink for everything coming down from room temperature. Every cable and pipe is clamped to it so the heat they conduct is dumped here, where cooling power is relatively plentiful, rather than further down. It also carries the 50 K radiation shield, which catches most of the heat glowing off the room-temperature vacuum can.
keyNumbers: Typically about 40 to 60 K
First pulse-tube stage can remove roughly tens of watts
Removes most of the heat load before it reaches colder stages
details.madeOf: Gold-plated oxygen-free copper. Very pure copper carries heat extremely well, so the whole plate stays at nearly the same temperature, and the thin gold layer stops the surface oxidising so bolted joints keep good thermal contact.

parts.name: 50 K plate

parts.description: Second pulse-tube stage at about 4 degrees above absolute zero, where the readout amplifiers sit.

details.didYouKnow: Helium-4 boils at about 4.2 K at normal air pressure, which is why older 'wet' fridges sat in a bath of liquid helium to reach this stage; today's 'dry' fridges make the same temperature with the pulse tube instead.
details.howItWorks: The 4 K plate sits on the pulse tube's second stage and is the last plate the cryocooler reaches directly; everything colder relies on the dilution unit. It hosts the readout amplifiers and their circulators, plus the first big attenuators on the incoming control lines. The returning helium mixture is also pre-cooled here before it heads down to condense.
keyNumbers: Typically about 3 to 4 K
Pulse-tube cooling power here is roughly 1 to 2 W
Each readout amplifier dissipates roughly a few milliwatts
details.madeOf: Gold-plated oxygen-free copper, like the other plates. Below about 10 K, pure copper becomes even better at carrying heat than it is at room temperature, so the plate evens out hot spots from the amplifiers.

parts.name: 4 K plate

parts.description: Stage at about 1 degree above absolute zero, cooled by the still where helium-3 is pumped away.

details.didYouKnow: Below about 2.2 K, helium-4 becomes a superfluid that flows without friction and can creep up walls as a thin film, so stills are designed to stop this film carrying helium-4 away with the helium-3.
details.howItWorks: The still plate is attached to the still, whose evaporating helium-3 keeps it below 1 K. Wires and the incoming helium line are anchored here to shed heat before going further down. Because the still has far more cooling power than the stages below it, intercepting heat here protects the delicate lowest stages.
keyNumbers: Typically about 0.7 to 1 K
Cooling power roughly a few to tens of milliwatts
Often carries an attenuator of about 10 dB on each control line
details.madeOf: Gold-plated oxygen-free copper. The gold plating keeps contact surfaces clean and slightly soft, so bolted joints press together closely and pass heat well.

parts.name: Still plate

parts.description: Intermediate stage at about a tenth of a degree, which intercepts heat flowing down the wires.

details.didYouKnow: At around a tenth of a kelvin, the heat that a single extra wire could carry from the stage above can be enough to noticeably warm a stage, so engineers count every cable.
details.howItWorks: The cold plate sits between the still and the mixing chamber and is cooled by the helium flowing through the heat exchangers. It is a stepping stone: wires, attenuators and filters are clamped to it so heat leaking down from the still plate is caught before reaching the mixing chamber, which has very little cooling power to spare. Supports and shields below hang from it.
keyNumbers: Typically about 100 mK
Cooling power roughly a few hundred microwatts
About 3,000 times colder than room temperature
details.madeOf: Gold-plated oxygen-free copper. At these temperatures even tiny heat leaks matter, so a pure, well-annealed copper plate with clean gold contacts is used to spread and sink heat efficiently.

parts.name: Cold plate

parts.description: Coldest plate, around 10 thousandths of a degree above absolute zero; the processor hangs below it.

details.didYouKnow: Deep space glows at about 2.7 K, so the mixing chamber plate is roughly two hundred times colder than the empty space between galaxies.
details.howItWorks: The mixing chamber plate is bolted directly to the mixing chamber and is the coldest large surface in the fridge. The cold finger, processor package and final attenuators, filters and parametric amplifiers hang from it. Its temperature is read by specialised thermometers, because measuring a few thousandths of a kelvin accurately is itself a challenge.
keyNumbers: Typically about 10 to 15 mK in operation
Cooling power roughly 10 to 20 microwatts at 20 mK
Cooling down from room temperature typically takes a day or more
details.madeOf: Gold-plated oxygen-free copper, chosen for its high purity so it conducts heat well even at millikelvin temperatures. Thermometers here are often ruthenium-oxide resistors whose resistance rises steeply as they cool.

parts.name: Mixing chamber plate

parts.description: Thin, hollow rods that hold each plate below the one above while letting as little heat as possible flow down them.

details.didYouKnow: The heat that leaks down a support grows with its cross-section and shrinks with its length, so the posts are made as long, thin and hollow as the weight they carry allows.
details.howItWorks: Posts like these connect each plate to the one above, holding the stack rigidly in line while acting as deliberate bottlenecks for heat. Heat flowing down a rod depends on how well its material conducts, how big its cross-section is and how long it is, so they are made thin-walled, hollow and from poor heat conductors. They must still be stiff enough to stop the stack swaying or vibrating.
keyNumbers: Usually several posts between each pair of plates
Stainless steel conducts heat over a thousand times worse than pure copper at a few kelvin
Walls typically only a millimetre or so thick
details.madeOf: Typically thin-walled tubes of stainless steel, titanium alloy or glass-fibre composite such as G-10. These materials are strong but conduct heat very badly at low temperatures, which is exactly what is wanted.

parts.name: Support posts

parts.description: Rotary valve on top that sends pulses of high-pressure helium gas down the pulse tube about once a second.

details.didYouKnow: The steady rhythmic hiss of the valve and compressor is one of the most recognisable sounds in a quantum computing lab, and the compressor usually needs its own water cooling to carry away its heat.
details.howItWorks: A separate compressor, often in another room, supplies high-pressure helium gas through flexible hoses. The motor turns a rotary valve that switches the pulse tube between the high- and low-pressure lines, creating rhythmic pressure waves inside the cooler. Those pressure swings, timed against the gas flow, are what pump heat up and out of the cold stages.
keyNumbers: Pulses roughly 1 to 2 times per second
High-side helium pressure typically about 20 bar
Compressor typically draws roughly 7 to 10 kW
details.madeOf: A cast and machined metal valve body with a small electric motor and a rotating valve disc. The motor is often mounted slightly away from the cold head on a flexible line so its vibration is not passed into the fridge.

parts.name: Pulse-tube valve motor

parts.description: Two-stage cooler with no moving parts in the cold, chilling the 50 K and 4 K plates by expanding helium gas.

details.didYouKnow: Because nothing moves at the cold end, pulse tubes vibrate far less than older cryocoolers, and their spread from the 2000s onwards made helium-free 'dry' dilution fridges the norm.
details.howItWorks: Helium gas is squeezed and released in pulses, and a regenerator packed with fine material stores and returns heat on each cycle. Gas compressed at the warm end gives up heat there; gas expanding at the cold end absorbs heat, so the bottom of each stage gets steadily colder. The first stage cools the 50 K plate and the second the 4 K plate, and the returning helium mixture is also pre-cooled on its way down.
keyNumbers: Two stages: roughly 50 K and 4 K
Cooling power roughly 1 to 2 W at 4 K
Roughly 40 W of cooling at the first stage on larger models
details.madeOf: Thin-walled stainless-steel tubes with copper heat stations at each stage. The lower regenerator is packed with special rare-earth compounds that still store heat well at a few kelvin, where ordinary metals almost cannot.

parts.name: Pulse-tube cooler

parts.description: Chamber where helium-3 evaporates out of the mixture and is pumped away, driving the circulation.

details.didYouKnow: Helium-3 is extremely rare and mostly comes as a by-product of the radioactive decay of tritium, so the few litres of gas in a fridge's mixture can be worth thousands of dollars per litre.
details.howItWorks: Inside the still, a liquid helium mixture is pumped on by vacuum pumps at room temperature. Helium-3 evaporates far more readily than helium-4 here, so the gas pumped away is mostly helium-3. Removing it pulls more helium-3 up out of the mixing chamber, which keeps the cooling cycle running; the gas is then cleaned, compressed and sent back down to condense again. A small heater lets operators speed the flow up.
keyNumbers: Typically about 0.7 K
Pumped vapour usually more than 90 percent helium-3
Still heater typically adds a few milliwatts
details.madeOf: Copper, so heat moves easily between the liquid inside and the still plate. Its pumping line is wide, because gas at such low pressure flows sluggishly and needs a generous path out.

parts.name: Still

parts.description: Coiled tubes where the cold helium leaving the mixing chamber pre-cools the warmer helium coming in.

details.didYouKnow: The resistance to heat crossing a boundary between helium and metal, called Kapitza resistance, grows sharply as temperature falls, which is the main reason dilution fridge heat exchangers are so elaborate.
details.howItWorks: Liquid helium-3 heading to the mixing chamber has to be cooled almost to the mixing chamber's own temperature, or it would warm it up. In the heat exchangers it flows past the very cold dilute mixture travelling the other way, back up to the still, so the two streams swap heat. This counter-flow trick means the incoming helium arrives already very cold.
keyNumbers: Spans roughly 1 K down to about 10 mK
Silver powder grains typically well under a micrometre
Total contact area can be many square metres
details.madeOf: Fine tube-in-tube coils of stainless steel or copper-nickel, followed by blocks filled with sintered silver powder. The powder gives an enormous surface area, which is needed because heat has great difficulty crossing from metal into liquid helium at these temperatures.

parts.name: Heat exchangers

parts.description: The coldest point: helium-3 atoms cross from a concentrated layer into a dilute one, absorbing heat as they go.

details.didYouKnow: Because helium-3 stays dissolved in helium-4 even at absolute zero, there is always somewhere for it to cross into, which is why this cooling method keeps working at temperatures where evaporation has all but stopped.
details.howItWorks: Below about 0.87 K, a helium-3 and helium-4 mixture separates into two liquid layers: a helium-3 rich layer floating on a dilute one. Pumping at the still draws helium-3 out of the dilute layer, so atoms from the rich layer cross the boundary to replace them. Crossing takes energy, much like evaporation, so each crossing absorbs heat. The dilution refrigerator was proposed by Heinz London and first built in the mid-1960s.
keyNumbers: Base temperature typically below about 10 mK
Dilute layer holds about 6.6 percent helium-3 even near absolute zero
Helium-3 circulation typically hundreds of micromoles per second
details.madeOf: High-purity copper, often with sintered silver inside to help heat pass into the liquid. It is bolted firmly to the mixing chamber plate so that everything below shares its temperature.

parts.name: Mixing chamber

parts.description: Semi-rigid coaxial cables carrying microwave control pulses down and qubit signals back up, cooled at every plate.

details.didYouKnow: To fit more qubits, researchers are developing flat flexible ribbon cables that pack many microwave lines side by side, because round coax takes up too much room in the fridge.
details.howItWorks: Each coaxial line has an inner conductor surrounded by insulation and a metal outer shield, guiding microwave pulses without leaking or picking up interference. Control lines carry pulses down to the qubits; readout lines bring the qubits' replies back up. At every plate the line is clamped to a heat sink so its heat is removed in stages. Large processors need several lines per qubit, so wiring is one of the hardest parts of scaling up.
keyNumbers: Outer diameter typically about 0.9 to 2.2 mm
Niobium-titanium superconducts below roughly 10 K
Large systems can need hundreds of lines
details.madeOf: Semi-rigid cable with outer and inner conductors of stainless steel or copper-nickel in the warmer sections, which carry heat poorly. Readout lines below 4 K often use superconducting niobium-titanium, which loses almost no signal and conducts very little heat.

parts.name: Coaxial lines

parts.description: Small inline blocks on the incoming lines that soak up thermal noise from warmer stages before it reaches the chip.

details.didYouKnow: A control signal can arrive at the chip a million times weaker than it was at the top of the fridge, which is fine because qubits need only a tiny amount of microwave power.
details.howItWorks: Room-temperature electronics produce microwave noise simply from being warm, and that noise would heat the qubits and scramble them. An attenuator absorbs most of the power passing through it and re-emits only the faint noise of its own, much colder, temperature. Placing them at several stages steps the noise down; the control signals are sent in strong enough to survive the losses.
keyNumbers: Typically about 20 dB each at 4 K and the mixing chamber
20 dB cuts the power by a factor of 100
Total roughly 60 dB down a control line
details.madeOf: A thin-film resistor network inside a small metal body, often gold-plated brass, copper or stainless steel. The body is bolted tightly to a plate, because the energy it absorbs turns into heat that must be removed.

parts.name: Attenuators

parts.description: Low-noise transistor amplifiers on the 4 K plate that boost the qubits' faint signals before they leave the fridge.

details.didYouKnow: The HEMT was invented around 1980 at Fujitsu, and similar transistors are used in radio telescopes and satellite dishes to pick up very faint signals.
details.howItWorks: A qubit is measured by bouncing a weak microwave tone off a small resonator coupled to it, and the reply is far too faint to send straight up the cables. The HEMT, a high electron mobility transistor, boosts it at 4 K, where it adds very little noise of its own. Many systems also put a quantum-limited parametric amplifier, such as a travelling-wave type, at the mixing chamber to boost the signal first.
keyNumbers: Gain typically about 35 to 40 dB
Added noise equivalent to just a few kelvin
Power use roughly a few milliwatts each
details.madeOf: Transistors made from layered semiconductors such as indium phosphide or gallium arsenide, where electrons travel in an ultra-thin sheet with little scattering. They sit in a machined metal housing with connectors and DC bias wires.

parts.name: Readout amplifiers

parts.description: Magnetic one-way valves for microwaves that let signals travel up to the amplifiers but stop noise travelling back down.

details.didYouKnow: Because they contain magnets, circulators must be kept at a distance or shielded from the qubits, and researchers are working on magnet-free superconducting versions that could be built onto chips.
details.howItWorks: A circulator has three ports and passes microwaves only in one rotational direction, from port one to two, two to three, and so on. Terminating one port with a resistor makes an isolator, which lets signals travel up from the qubits but absorbs noise and reflections coming back down from the amplifiers. Two are often used in series for extra protection.
keyNumbers: Isolation typically about 20 dB each
Operating band typically around 4 to 8 GHz
Three ports on a circulator, two on an isolator
details.madeOf: A disc of ferrite, a magnetic ceramic such as yttrium iron garnet, held in the field of small permanent magnets inside a metal housing. The magnetised ferrite treats waves differently depending on which way they travel, which is what makes it one-way.

parts.name: Isolators & circulators

parts.description: Gold-plated copper rod that hangs the processor below the mixing chamber plate and keeps it at the same temperature.

details.didYouKnow: At these temperatures, the quality of a bolted joint matters as much as the metal: joints are often tightened with special washers so they stay tight as the parts shrink while cooling.
details.howItWorks: The cold finger extends the mixing chamber plate's cold downward so the processor can sit lower in the fridge, inside its own magnetic shield and away from components like circulators. It acts as a short, very good thermal path, so the chip package stays within a whisker of the plate's temperature. It also gives a firm mechanical mount so the package does not swing.
keyNumbers: Typically about 10 to 20 mK, close to the plate
Copper purity typically about 99.99 percent
Usually tens of centimetres long
details.madeOf: Gold-plated oxygen-free copper. Annealed high-purity copper conducts heat extremely well at millikelvin temperatures, and the gold stops oxide forming at bolted joints that would otherwise block heat.

parts.name: Cold finger

parts.description: Nested cans of special nickel-iron alloy and superconducting metal that keep magnetic fields away from the qubits. Drawn with a slice removed to show the package.

details.didYouKnow: A superconductor freezes in whatever field it has as it cools through its transition, so fridges are cooled with the shields already in place to lock in as little field as possible.
details.howItWorks: Stray magnetic fields, including the Earth's own, can shift qubit frequencies and get trapped in superconducting circuits as tiny whirlpools of current called vortices, which cause energy loss. The outer high-permeability can soaks up field lines and channels them around the inside. An inner superconducting can goes further: once cold, it expels changes in magnetic field entirely.
keyNumbers: Earth's field is roughly 50 microtesla
Shielding typically reduces it by a factor of hundreds or more
Mu-metal is roughly 80 percent nickel
details.madeOf: Nickel-iron alloys such as mu-metal, or versions specially treated to work at low temperatures, plus cans of superconducting aluminium or lead. The alloys need careful heat treatment, because bending or knocking them reduces their shielding.

parts.name: Magnetic shield

parts.description: Gold-plated copper enclosure with microwave connectors round its edge, holding the chip and shielding it from stray radiation.

details.didYouKnow: A single stray infrared photon can break apart the paired electrons that let a superconductor carry current, so even tiny light leaks into the package can measurably shorten qubit lifetimes.
details.howItWorks: The chip sits in a pocket in the package and is connected to a small circuit board by fine wire bonds or, in newer designs, by bump bonds. Coaxial connectors round the edge link each line to the outside. The closed metal box blocks stray infrared light and must be shaped so its own internal microwave resonances do not land near the qubit frequencies.
keyNumbers: Typically several to dozens of connectors
Wire bonds about 25 micrometres thick
Box resonances usually pushed well above about 8 GHz
details.madeOf: Gold-plated oxygen-free copper or sometimes superconducting aluminium, with a low-loss circuit board inside. Some designs coat inside surfaces with infrared-absorbing material to soak up any stray light.

parts.name: Processor package

parts.description: Chip of tiny superconducting aluminium circuits on silicon or sapphire; each qubit is an oscillating loop of current.

details.didYouKnow: In 2019, a 53-qubit chip of this kind performed a sampling task in about 200 seconds that was claimed to take a top supercomputer thousands of years, though better classical methods later narrowed that gap.
details.howItWorks: Each transmon qubit is a tiny electrical circuit with a Josephson junction, two layers of superconductor separated by a barrier only a few atoms thick, which behaves like a non-linear inductor. That makes its energy levels unevenly spaced, so the lowest two can serve as a 0 and 1. Microwave pulses tuned to each qubit's frequency rotate its state, and couplers let neighbours interact to perform two-qubit operations. The transmon design was introduced in 2007.
keyNumbers: Qubit frequencies typically about 4 to 8 GHz
Gate pulses typically tens of nanoseconds
Coherence times typically tens to a few hundred microseconds
Dozens to over a hundred qubits per chip
details.madeOf: Aluminium and sometimes niobium or tantalum circuits patterned on a silicon or sapphire chip, with aluminium oxide forming the junction barriers. Aluminium becomes superconducting below about 1.2 K and forms a very clean oxide.

parts.name: Quantum processor chip

parts.description: Can hanging from the 4 K plate that blocks heat radiated by the warmer shield outside it. Drawn with a slice removed to show the stages inside.

details.didYouKnow: Some fridges add a further shield at the still stage inside this one, so the processor is wrapped in several nested cans, each colder than the last.
details.howItWorks: Every warm surface glows with infrared heat, and the amount rises steeply with temperature. The 4 K shield surrounds the coldest stages so they only see a surface at about 4 K, rather than the 50 K shield outside, cutting the radiated heat they receive to almost nothing. Small holes and gaps are sealed carefully, as stray infrared reaching the qubits harms their performance.
keyNumbers: Held at roughly 3 to 4 K
Radiated heat scales with the fourth power of temperature
Typically tens of centimetres across
details.madeOf: Aluminium or copper, which reflect infrared well and spread heat evenly to the 4 K plate. Inside surfaces are sometimes blackened with infrared-absorbing coatings so any stray light is caught rather than bouncing around.

parts.name: 4 K radiation shield

parts.description: Larger aluminium can on the 50 K plate, the first barrier against room-temperature heat radiation. Drawn with a slice removed to show the stages inside.

details.didYouKnow: Multilayer insulation is the same idea used on spacecraft, where the shiny gold or silver blankets on satellites protect them from the Sun's heat.
details.howItWorks: The 50 K shield is the first barrier between the cold stack and the room-temperature vacuum can. It soaks up the infrared glow from the can and passes that heat to the pulse tube's first stage, which has far more cooling power to deal with it. Without it, the 4 K stage would be swamped by radiated heat.
keyNumbers: Held at roughly 40 to 60 K
Receives roughly a thousand times less radiation at 50 K than at room temperature
Typically the largest of the inner cans
details.madeOf: Aluminium, which is light, reflective and conducts heat well. It is often wrapped in multilayer insulation, many thin sheets of aluminised plastic film that each reflect back a little more of the heat.

parts.name: 50 K radiation shield

parts.description: Outer steel can bolted to the top plate; pumping the air out stops gas carrying heat to the cold stages. Drawn with a slice removed to show the stages inside.

details.didYouKnow: When a system is opened up for work, the cans are lowered off the stack one by one, which is why quantum computers are usually photographed as the open gold chandelier rather than the plain cylinder they look like when running.
details.howItWorks: Air would carry heat to the cold parts by collisions between gas molecules, so the can is sealed to the top plate and pumped out before cooling. Once the inside gets cold, any remaining gas freezes onto cold surfaces, improving the vacuum further. The can must also withstand the full weight of the atmosphere pressing on its outside.
keyNumbers: Pumped to roughly a millionth of a millibar or better
Air pushes on it with about 10 tonnes-force per square metre
Often a metre or more tall
details.madeOf: Stainless steel or aluminium, sealed with rubber O-rings at the top flange. These metals are strong enough to resist atmospheric pressure and release very little trapped gas into the vacuum.

parts.name: Outer vacuum can

parts.description: Flexible braids of pure copper that carry heat from the plates into the pulse tube's cold flanges without passing on its vibration.

details.didYouKnow: A joint can matter as much as the braid: a badly tightened bolt can leave a plate several degrees warmer than it should be, which is why the bolts are often torqued with special washers that keep their grip as everything shrinks.
details.howItWorks: The pulse tube makes cold at its two flanges, but the plates are where the cold is needed. These braids join the two, carrying heat out of the plates along hundreds of fine copper strands. Because the braid is floppy, the small shudder of each helium pulse dies out in it instead of shaking the plates, the wiring and in the end the qubits.
keyNumbers: Usually several braids per stage
Carries roughly tens of watts at the first stage
Carries roughly a watt or two at 4 K
details.madeOf: Woven strands of very pure copper, crimped and soldered into solid copper end blocks, then bolted down with the contact faces cleaned or gold-plated. Pure copper carries heat especially well when it is cold.

parts.name: Copper heat straps

parts.description: The wide pumping line that draws helium-3 vapour up from the still, and the thin line that returns it, condensed, towards the mixing chamber.

details.didYouKnow: The whole fridge holds only a modest amount of helium-3, an extremely scarce isotope mostly obtained from the decay of tritium, so the gas is kept in a sealed circuit and never vented.
details.howItWorks: Pumps at room temperature pull helium-3 vapour up the wide line from the still, keeping it evaporating. The gas is cleaned, compressed and sent back down the thin line, where it is condensed to a liquid at about 4 K and cooled further on its way to the mixing chamber. The two lines close the loop that keeps the refrigerator running continuously.
keyNumbers: Pumping line typically several centimetres across
Return line typically a few millimetres across
Helium-3 flow typically hundreds of micromoles per second
details.madeOf: Thin-walled stainless steel, which conducts little heat, with flexible bellows that allow for shrinking as it cools. The wide line has to be generous because the vapour is at very low pressure.

parts.name: Helium circulation lines

parts.description: First amplifier the qubits' signal meets, right beside the chip on the coldest plate, adding almost no noise of its own.

details.didYouKnow: Quantum mechanics sets a hard floor on how quiet an ordinary amplifier can be: half a photon of added noise. These devices come close to that floor.
details.howItWorks: A qubit's readout signal is only a few microwave photons, far too faint for the transistor amplifiers higher up. This amplifier boosts it right away by borrowing energy from a strong pump tone, using superconducting junctions whose behaviour changes with the current through them. Since it dissipates almost nothing and adds close to the minimum noise quantum physics allows, the signal comes out large enough to survive the rest of the trip.
keyNumbers: Gain typically about 20 dB
Operates at around 10 to 20 mK
Added noise close to half a photon
details.madeOf: A superconducting aluminium or niobium circuit on a small chip with many Josephson junctions, in a gold-plated copper box with microwave connectors and usually its own magnetic shielding.

parts.name: Quantum-limited amplifier

summary: A superconducting quantum computer: a gold-plated 'chandelier' of cooling stages that takes a tiny processor chip down to about a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero, wired with coaxial lines that carry microwave pulses in and faint signals out.
